Main finding
The recommended settings for the as-loaded forecast are half steps with first level selection and max_iters equal 
to 400. They achieve worst-day availability of 18 aircraft and smoothness of 1.391860, a 1.56 percent reduction 
in standard deviation from the default. Mean availability remains 21.713010 aircraft.
Worst-day availability of 18 is globally maximal under the first D check rules for this forecast. Six aircraft must be 
in D maintenance together on six dates in May 2033. Tuning therefore improves the distribution of availability 
around an already optimal worst day. The best smoothness found is an empirical result; the study does not 
establish a global smoothness optimum.

Priority based selection | 2
Algorithm and hyperparameters
The baseline is a deterministic hill-climb using a sequence of neighbourhoods. For each neighbourhood, checks 
are ordered by the lowest availability during their active maintenance interval. The search scans priority levels 
from worst to best and stops at the first level containing an improving move. It then accepts the best move 
within that level and starts the next iteration at the first neighbourhood again.
A proposal moves one check by an offset and rebuilds the aircraft's later checks. Rebuilds enforce the 
maintenance sequence and recalculate due dates and legal start windows. Positive offsets may move a check 
later within its legal window; no check may start after its current due date. A larger improving shift can cross 
over schedules that are worse, but the algorithm never accepts a worsening endpoint.

Shift magnitude in days 28 14 7 3 1 to 70
Neighbourhood structure Four pairs Pairs half offsets unions asymmetric sets
Neighbourhood order Large to small Reversed interleaved and refined ladders
Selection policy First priority level First level all levels first improving
What is and is not tunable
Only max_iters is exposed by savn_optimise. shift_sets is a local constant in that function, and first-priority-level 
selection is built into generate_neighbors. This study varies these algorithm settings in a separate driver. 
Temperature, cooling rate, tabu tenure, and a search random seed do not apply to this deterministic method.
Objective and fixed inputs
Scores are compared lexicographically as (minimum availability, negative standard deviation, mean availability). 
A gain of one aircraft on the worst day outranks any smoothness change. Standard deviation uses the population 
definition implemented by numpy.std. No weighted scalar objective is introduced.
Maintenance rules are fixed domain inputs: A 14 day duration 365 day interval 42 day early allowance; B 28 730 70; C 84 1460 70; D 126 
2920 70. Changing these rules would change the scheduling problem rather than tune the optimiser.

A single plus-or-minus seven-day neighbourhood is the strongest converged single-magnitude setting in this 
sweep. It reaches 18 available aircraft but ends at standard deviation 1.470754, worse than the default and 
tuned ladders. A fourteen-day neighbourhood also reaches 18 quickly, after 188 accepted moves, but leaves 
standard deviation 1.474391.
The one-, two-, and three-day searches hit the 400-move cap at worst-day availability 17. These results show 
inefficient progress within the tested budget; they do not establish that the small-step neighbourhoods would 
converge at 17. The five-day run also hits its cap, even though it reaches 18.
Very wide single steps are poor on this workbook. The seventy-day setting accepts only two moves and 
converges at 15, while fifty-six days converges at 16. Wide jumps often lie outside legal windows or offer no 
improving endpoint. That explanation is consistent with the outcome but the historical study did not count 
rejected proposals, so it is not a measured rejection-rate result.
Implication for tuning
Retain multiple scales of movement. The strongest single neighbourhood does not replace a ladder, and larger 
offsets do not monotonically improve the result. Fine offsets are useful for later smoothness improvement when 
combined with earlier larger shifts.

Half offsets within each neighbourhood
The previous tuned baseline uses four neighbourhoods: (-28, -14, 14, 28), (-14, -7, 7, 14), (-7, -3, 3, 7), and (-3, -1, 
1, 3). The best improving move is selected among all offsets within the first improving priority level. This 
produces a different trajectory from trying each offset pair in a separate neighbourhood.
A single union of the original offsets returns standard deviation 1.413656. Adding 21- and one-day offsets to that 
union reaches 1.406534. Both are worse than the half-step ladder. This is measured evidence for retaining the 
layered search structure on this input, rather than a general guarantee that layering always wins.

First level returns all improving candidates in the first priority level that contains any, then takes the best. All 
levels takes the best improving candidate across every priority level for the active neighbourhood. First 
improving stops at the first improving candidate in priority level, start date, aircraft name, check index, and 
offset order. All three still require a strictly better lexicographic score.
The interaction table tests each policy on three different neighbourhood structures. This avoids assuming that a 
selection rule measured on the default transfers unchanged to the tuned ladder. Ties in candidate scores retain 
the first candidate in the deterministic iteration order.
The best endpoint in this interaction comparison uses half steps with first level selection and standard deviation 
1.391860. The report recommends settings based on the complete extended comparison, including local 
refinements, rather than treating the selection comparison as a separate optimisation target.
Priority sorting directs proposals towards checks that cover low-availability days, but it is a search heuristic. Even 
all-level selection preserves worst-day availability through the score rule. Any smoothness differences arise from 
different accepted paths, not from one policy allowing worse worst days.
Fresh results use the same 800 safety cap. Historical default all-level selection ended at 1.415233; half-step all-level selection ended at 
1.403198. Reproduced endpoints provide an additional consistency check.

Priority based selection | 13
Availability limits and operational scope
The mean is fixed by conserved total downtime. Over 4481 days, the 278 checks require 10248 aircraft days of 
maintenance, so mean availability is 24 minus 10248 divided by 4481, or 21.713010489. Changing only legal 
starts cannot improve the mean when all checks stay inside the comparison horizon. The third score component 
therefore does not discriminate among these runs.
Why worst day availability cannot exceed 18
Each aircraft's first D due date is its first A due date plus 2555 days. A, B, and C checks do not reset the D due 
clock. The first D duration is 126 days and its early allowance is 70 days. A D check with due day d can start only 
between d minus 70 and d. Every legal placement occupies the forced interval from d to d plus 56, with the end 
excluded.
Aircraft D due date Last forced day
Aircraft 11 01 May 2033 25 Jun 2033
Aircraft 14 05 May 2033 29 Jun 2033
Aircraft 15 31 Mar 2033 25 May 2033
Aircraft 19 20 May 2033 14 Jul 2033
Aircraft 24 16 Apr 2033 10 Jun 2033
Blue-8 02 Apr 2033 27 May 2033
These six forced intervals overlap on 20 to 25 May 2033. At least six aircraft must be unavailable on each of these 
dates, so at most 18 can be available. Since the tuned schedules achieve a worst day of 18 across the whole 
horizon, the primary objective is proven optimal for this forecast and the unchanged first D rules.
This bound does not prove the best possible smoothness at minimum 18. A different neighbourhood or a search 
that accepts intermediate worsening schedules could still improve standard deviation. Reaching 19 would 
require changing a problem assumption, such as the D early allowance, first due clocks, or check duration, and 
must be treated as a separate scenario.
Operational constraints
The baseline validates maintenance rules, legal starts, non-overlap, and the horizon. It does not load 
operational_constraints.json and does not enforce busy periods, dependency groups, or displacement limits. A 
tuned schedule must be re-evaluated under any required operational constraints before it is used as an 
operational plan. Hyperparameter rankings under added constraints may differ.

Implementation and reproducibility
Applying the recommendation
The production module and source workbook remain unchanged. To apply the recommended neighbourhoods in 
savn_optimise, replace the local shift_sets list with the neighbourhoods listed on the local refinement page. 
Preserve maintenance rebuilds and lexicographic acceptance. If the recommended policy is first level, no 
generate_neighbors change is needed; alternative policies require the corresponding study selection behaviour 
to be made explicit.
Expose shift_sets as a function argument for repeatable comparison rather than editing a local constant for 
every experiment. Keep the frozen default as the default argument for baseline comparisons. Record the chosen 
cap, the accepted-move count, and whether the search stopped naturally. An 800 cap provides room for the 
observed start-schedule sensitivity experiments without requiring 800 moves.
Reproducing the evidence
Run .scratch/priority-hyperparameter-analysis/run_analysis.py with the Python runtime listed in the source 
record. The script resumes completed trials only when source workbook and production hashes match. To force 
a clean rerun, use a fresh study folder or preserve and rename the existing fresh-results.json before running 
again. The original study also skips existing names and must not be mistaken for a fresh execution when rerun 
against its stored file.
fresh-results.json contains complete endpoint metrics, daily distributions, hashes, and accepted-move 
trajectories. Each fresh run also has a schedule JSON; start_41.json, start_42.json, and start_43.json preserve the 
sensitivity inputs. analysis-summary.json records combined counts and the selected configuration. The historical 
run table and fresh catalogue follow in the appendices.
Limits of the recommendation
This study covers one 24-aircraft forecast and three small legal perturbations of it. It does not test an 
independent fleet, a different horizon, larger data, changed maintenance rules, or operational constraints. The 
search is deterministic and the setting sweep is deliberately selected rather than exhaustive. The measured best 
is a tuned baseline for this problem, and future method comparisons should report comparable outcomes and 
budgets against it.
The start-variant medians describe sensitivity across three fixed inputs. Timing medians describe three repeated 
executions of one deterministic input. Neither supports statistical significance claims. Report a cap-limited 
endpoint as incomplete convergence and avoid selecting settings solely from smoothness when their worst-day 
availability is lower.
